what: BGC Group is a broker between financial institutions. Its people and electronic platforms match buyers and sellers of interest rate products, foreign exchange, credit, energy and commodities, taking a commission without holding the positions themselves. It also owns the FMX exchange venture.
customers: Banks, hedge funds, asset managers and corporate treasuries trading in markets where there is no central exchange and a broker is needed to find the other side.
money: Rates, credit and foreign exchange brokerage
Commissions on brokered trades in fixed income, credit and currency markets.
Brokerage in energy, shipping and commodity markets.
Market data sold from the trades it brokers, and the FMX exchange venture.
moat: Inter-dealer broking is a network business: the broker who sees the most flow knows where the other side is, which attracts more flow. The data generated is a valuable by-product sold to people who need prices in markets with no public tape. FMX is an attempt to build a genuine exchange, which would be a far better business than broking if it works.
risks: Only two analysts are reflected in the $16.00 average target, so there is almost no external coverage of a $5.2B company.
Debt of $2.0B against $851.5M of cash is meaningful, and the FMX venture requires continued investment before it earns anything.
Brokerage revenue depends on trading volumes, which fall when markets are quiet.
Reported net income of $232.9M on $3.4B of revenue is a 6.8% margin, because broker compensation consumes most of the revenue.
FMX is competing against CME, which has one of the strongest network positions in global finance — a very hard target.
opportunities: Revenue has grown strongly, from $1.8B in 2022 to $2.9B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $3.4B.
Free cash flow of $553.1M against a $5.2B market value is a 10.6% yield, and the shares trade at about 9.5 times free cash flow.
Market volatility increases trading volumes, which makes the business countercyclical to calm markets rather than to the economy.
The data business monetises the same trades a second time at high margins.
If FMX succeeds in taking even a small share of interest rate futures, the economics would be far better than broking.
watch: Brokerage revenue by product and FMX volumes. The broking business is cyclical and understood; FMX is the option that could change what this company is worth.
view: BGC has two quite different things inside it. The first is a conventional inter-dealer broker: people and screens matching institutional buyers and sellers in markets with no central exchange, earning a commission. It is a decent network business — the broker who sees the most flow knows where the other side is — but most of the revenue goes out as broker compensation, which is why a $3.4 billion revenue business earns a 6.8% net margin.

The second is FMX, an attempt to build a genuine exchange for interest rate futures and US Treasuries. That is strategically the most interesting thing here by a wide margin, because an exchange is a vastly better business than broking: once liquidity concentrates, the margins are enormous and the position is nearly unassailable. It is also an extremely hard thing to do, because the incumbent is CME, whose network in interest rate futures is among the strongest in global finance. Liquidity does not move for a small price advantage.

The cyclicality of the base business is worth understanding properly, because it is unusual. Broking revenue rises with trading volumes, and volumes rise with volatility and uncertainty. That makes BGC countercyclical to calm markets rather than to the economy — it does well when central banks are moving rates, when credit is repricing, when currencies are unstable. Revenue going from $1.8 billion to $3.4 billion reflects exactly that period.

At 9.5 times free cash flow with a 10.6% yield, you are paying a broking multiple and getting the FMX option attached. Two analysts covering a $5.2 billion company means essentially nobody is examining this. My view is that the base business is fairly priced and FMX is genuinely free in the valuation — which is appropriate, because the probability of beating CME at its own game is low, and the payoff if it happens is very large. Watch FMX volumes; everything else here is the cycle.
bull: Volatility keeps broking volumes high while FMX takes even a small share of interest rate futures, turning a 9.5 times free cash flow broker into an exchange owner.
bear: Markets calm down and broking volumes fall, FMX never achieves liquidity against CME, and the investment in it keeps consuming cash.
